implementation_notes: Calling an async function returns a new Promise immediately; its body runs synchronously through the first incomplete await and then resumes through the job queue, so the language expresses both halves of the pattern directly: `const pending = work()` is the start-now step and `const value = await pending` is the collect step, without blocking the single-threaded event loop. Promise.all/race/any/allSettled are the built-in collectors for several outstanding calls, a rejected promise is the failure channel (delivered as a thrown exception at the await site), and then/catch/finally are the same operation in callback position - the promise is already settled if the handler is attached later, so there is no race between completion and registration. The runtime is single-threaded: asynchrony here means not occupying the loop, so CPU-bound work belongs in node:worker_threads, and promises themselves cannot be cancelled - only the underlying operation, through AbortSignal, can.
pitfalls: An unhandled promise rejection is reported through the host's unhandled-rejection mechanism (Node policy/version and browser console behavior differ); every owned task needs an await, catch, or explicit error sink.
Promises cannot be cancelled: Promise.race with a timeout abandons only the wait, while the underlying operation keeps running unless an AbortSignal is passed to it.
CPU-bound work inside an async function still blocks the single event loop; only workers give real parallelism.
Repeatedly attaching handlers to one long-lived pending promise accumulates handlers that are never released - cancel the source instead.
await schedules a microtask even for a settled promise, so ordering between synchronous code and continuations is subtle and must not be relied on.

variants.name: Error-first callback (Node.js classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-promise realization, still the contract of older Node.js APIs: the asynchronous function takes a final callback argument and returns immediately, and the callback receives (error, value) when the operation finishes - the callback is the completion notification and the collection step at once, and the err-first argument is the failure channel. Promisification (util.promisify) adapts it to the async/await variant. Write it only where the surrounding API is callback-based; new code should prefer promises, because callbacks invert the control flow, lose try/catch, and nest when several calls depend on each other.
pitfalls: The callback runs on the event loop, not at the call site: any context it needs (request state, transaction, cancellation flag) must be captured explicitly.
Calling the callback twice, or both the error and the value path, corrupts the caller's state - notification must be exactly once.
Throwing inside a callback escapes to the loop as an uncaught exception and does not reach the original caller's try/catch.
Deeply dependent calls nest and lose both error handling and ordering guarantees; this is precisely what promises replaced.
